summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the statute adopted in France in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, making transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.
tangentialFactors:
Opposition to the 2013 marriage reform came from organised religion as well as politics: the Catholic Bishops Conference in France came out against the adoption provisions of the bill, the record that accompanied the statute reaching Réunion.

Protection against 'identité sexuelle' discrimination entered the Penal Code through a harassment bill rather than a statute written for trans people, so the trans-specific wording depends on a general anti-harassment instrument.

Legal gender change was secured by parliamentary amendment rather than by executive decree, which is why the scope of the inserted Civil Code section remains sensitive to legislative sub-amendments.
localsOnly:
Residents of Réunion petition the French courts for legal gender change under the Civil Code section adopted on 19 May 2016; the same procedure, and the same documentation requirements, apply as in any French department.

Harassment or discriminatory treatment grounded in 'identité sexuelle' is prosecutable for residents under Penal Code article L225-1, in force since July 2012.

Residents detained in Réunion are assigned to prison accommodation by the sex recorded on their identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, the rule the CGLPL examined in its 25 May 2021 opinion.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved on this inventory: whether the CGLPL's recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries have been carried out in Réunion specifically, and whether any transgender detainees have been held in custody facilities in the department. The opinion is national; no local implementation data is sourced here.

The precise scope of the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282 after the government's three sub-amendments is not settled by these sources, so the conditions a resident must meet for legal gender change are not stated.

No source in this inventory records enforcement outcomes for 'identité sexuelle' discrimination complaints in Réunion, or any recorded act of anti-trans violence in the department.
